text.p: Ukraine tried on Thursday to dampen suggestions that the "sarcophagus" around the Chernobyl power station's ruined fourth reactor posed a serious danger, despite recent higher readings of neutron radiation inside.

Senior officials issued a flurry of statements discounting Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko's contention on Tuesday that the increased levels last week had triggered a limited chain reaction within the cracking structure.
"I believe Mr Kostenko is mistaken. He is no specialist in nuclear energy," Volodymyr Horbulyn, secretary of Ukraine's Security Council, told a news conference.
"Neither he nor I were there when all this occurred. I am inclined to be less pessimistic about what is happening in the sarcophagus."

But Horbulyn, who helped develop nuclear missile launchers in Soviet Ukraine, said safety within the tomb remained the single biggest long-term threat to the former Soviet republic 10 years after the reactor exploded. Ukraine has promised to close Chernobyl's two working reactors by the year 2000.
Viktor Baryakhtar, Vice-President of the Academy of Sciences, told an Academy session that increased neutron radiation was a periodic occurrence inside the structure.
"The likelihood of a chain reaction occurring is virtually zero," Interfax Ukraine news agency quoted him as saying. "It's hard to understand why there is such a panic now."
Even Russia's Deputy Nuclear Energy Minister, Lev Ryabev, issued a statement saying the readings were nothing unusual.
Kostenko himself backtracked in a new statement, saying news reports had exaggerated the dangers. Even if a further nuclear reaction occurred, he said, it would be limited.

The statements appeared to be aimed at calming Ukrainians who are still skittish about nuclear safety 10 years after the sarcophagus was hurriedly erected in the aftermath of the world's worst civil nuclear accident.

Ukrainian officials have said rain seeping through 1,000 square metres (11,000 sq ft) of cracks in the tomb pushed up readings of neutron radiation by several times for a few hours. They have called for swifter efforts to replace the structure.
But Western experts have said the levels are still far below those required to produce an explosion.
"It is still completely unclear just what happened last week inside that sarcophagus," Patrick Michaille, a French nuclear safety expert working in Ukraine, told Reuters.

"Whatever the readings were, they were far, far below anything that could develop into a serious chain reaction and explosion. There are political considerations here too. The Ukrainians are still negotiating over closing the station."
Wealthy Group of Seven nations have pledged more than $3 billion to help finance the closure of Chernobyl's two reactors, which provide five percent of Ukraine's electricity.

But Ukraine says the money is not being released quickly enough. Officials also complain that Western experts place too much emphasis on overhauling Ukraine's inefficient energy network and have forgotten the dangers posed by the tomb.

A 1993 Franco-British project to build a new tomb has made no progress and Western officials say it has been virtually abandoned as too expensive at over $1 billion. The project is to be discussed at a G-7 meeting next month in Paris.
